title: Judge denies Minnesota's bid to compel the extradition of an ICE officer from Texas
description: A federal judge on Wednesday refused to order Texas to extradite an Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer charged with shooting a man and lying about it during the immigration crackdown in Minne...
fullText:
BROWNSVILLE, Texas (AP) — A federal judge on Wednesday refused to order Texas to extradite an Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer charged with shooting a man and lying about it during the immigration crackdown in Minneapolis.

U.S. District Judge Fernando Rodriguez Jr. wrote in an order that he couldn't prevent a county sheriff from releasing Christian Castro or order Texas Gov. Greg Abbott to sign his extradition warrant.

The Cameron County sheriff said he would release Castro on Thursday morning.

Castro is charged in Minnesota with assault and falsely reporting a crime in the Jan. 14 shooting of 24-year-old Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis.

Castro is accused of firing a gun through the front door of a Minneapolis home, shooting Sosa-Celis in the leg. Prosecutors say Castro also falsely accused Sosa-Celis and another man of attacking an ICE officer with a broom handle and a snow shovel.

After a Minnesota judge issued a nationwide warrant for Castro's arrest in May, authorities, including Minnesota's Bureau of Criminal Apprehension, arrested Castro in Cameron County on May 29. Minnesota authorities have sought his extradition since his arrest, but he remains in custody in Brownsville, Texas, a city bordering Mexico.

Under Texas law and barring extradition, Castro must be released after 90 days of detention, which is Thursday.

Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison filed a request for a temporary restraining order last week seeking to block Castro's release or to order his return to Minnesota.

Texas attorneys on Tuesday argued the judge could not rule on a decision that's still pending. Abbott has not denied the extradition. Instead he is waiting for the outcome of an internal state investigation considering whether Castro was legally a "fugitive" under the Extradition Clause, the lawyers said.

The judge wrote in Wednesday's order that the court can't yet step in.

"The Court concludes that it lacks subject matter jurisdiction because the case is not ripe for adjudication," the order read. "Minnesota cannot premise its causes of action on the allegation that Governor Abbott may violate those authorities in the future; it must prove that a violation has already occurred."

The judge said in his order that the extradition laws do not outline how long the Texas governor can take to make that decision.

Ellison said in a statement that his office would keep litigating the case but didn't specify what it would do next.

"I respectfully but strongly disagree with the court's order, which nonetheless acknowledges that Christian Castro is a flight risk, that Minnesota will be harmed if he is allowed to flee to Mexico, and that Governor Abbott's consideration of Minnesota's extradition request is of 'an atypically long duration' — to say the least," Ellison said in a statement.

Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty, whose office handles prosecutions in Minneapolis, said at a new conference that Abbott was unfairly harboring the former ICE agent.

"If Christian Castro walks out of the door of the jail tomorrow and disappears into Mexico, it will be the fault of one person: Governor Greg Abbott," Moriarty said.

Abbott's press secretary, Andrew Mahaleris, welcomed the ruling and said it was the governor's duty to carefully consider the merits of extradition requests.

"Today's order rebuffs Minnesota's efforts to conscript federal courts into commandeering the authority of Governor Abbott's office," Mahaleris said in a statement.

Abbott said last week he would not respond to the extradition request, citing the ongoing investigation into fraud in government social service programs in Minnesota, which President Donald Trump used to justify his immigration crackdown there.

Minnesota officials say Castro could flee the country, citing calls he made from jail to a woman in Mexico, talking "about marrying her and buying a house in Mexico when he is released," according to the lawsuit.

The judge conceded that Castro could flee the country but added that "the threat of injury by itself does not create an issue ripe for adjudication."

title: Liverpool's midfield is fragile - will they act in the window?
description: Liverpool's draw at Newcastle emphasised once again their midfield fragility but will they act in the market and bring in a defensive-minded player?
fullText:
A little over four minutes had passed at St James' Park on Sunday and Liverpool had started encouragingly, keeping the ball well and with urgency in their play.

Ryan Gravenberch created space with a brilliant touch to get past Lewis Miley but instead of shooting from the edge of the box or playing Dominik Szoboszlai through, the Netherlands international lost possession.

Just 11 seconds later, Newcastle were ahead through Anthony Elanga after a devastating counter that required one pass after Amar Dedic's initial clearance.

Liverpool simply had no structure when out of possession. It was schoolboy stuff and a nightmare start for Andoni Iraola.

It was a similar story in the second half when Gravenberch was dispossessed after trying a back heel on the edge of the Newcastle box.

This time, Yoane Wissa went on a brilliant run through the centre - evading an array of Liverpool players - and played the ball to Joe Willock, who finished in style.

As Iraola alluded to after, perhaps one of his players should have had the know how to commit a foul in that situation but Liverpool were punished again.

Looking back on both goals, Gravenberch's decision-making should have been better and perhaps the centre-back pairing of Virgil van Dijk and Jeremy Jacquet could have engaged quicker rather than holding off.

But having a defensive midfielder stationed accordingly would, in all likelihood, have nullified the threat.

Liverpool have not had an out-and-out number six since Fabinho, who left in 2023, and as it stands Iraola's preference is a two-man pivot in midfield with Florian Wirtz playing as a number 10.

Both of those two midfielders, Gravenberch and Szoboszlai, were in the Newcastle box when Liverpool lost possession before Elanga's opener.

If Liverpool are to be taken seriously, they simply cannot concede goals like that regularly.

Iraola tends to avoid major debriefs in the dressing room after a game, with his personal preference to speak to the players a day later.

Asked in his post-match news conference about what could be done to prevent the kind of goals his side conceded, the Liverpool head coach suggested that it was not due to the type or identity of midfielders he had selected.

"I think it's just not personnel," said Iraola. "I understand you are telling me basically that Ryan Gravenberch is the six and he is on the edge of the box - but if he shoots and he scores we are saying what a play from Ryan Gravenberch."

It was an interesting point, given that Gravenberch produced the assist for Cody Gakpo's equaliser.

But shortly after Newcastle went 2-1 up, Iraola reacted by bringing on Alexis Mac Allister for Wirtz and Liverpool did seem more stable defensively - even if the Argentina international prefers to play as an eight.

Szoboszlai made zero tackles and won three of his 10 duels (30%) while Gravenberch similarly failed to make a tackle and won four of his 10 duels (40%).

When Mac Allister came on, he made two tackles and won four of his five duels (80%).

"We have to adapt as a team to these situations and we have to know that these situations can happen," added Iraola.

"I think the second goal, we probably did better in terms of having the numbers to defend - we don't make the foul, or go to the first challenge or probably reduce the distance with the ball carrier, so it's an incredible goal.

"Situations [are] just not because one person is playing there, [it] is something that we have to correct between a lot of players."

At full-time, the xG was 1.43 to Newcastle and 2.73 to Liverpool - indicating Newcastle had ruthlessly seized their opportunities against Iraola's side.

On Sky Sports, former Liverpool striker Daniel Sturridge did not hold back in his criticism.

"Liverpool do not have that profile of player right now." said Sturridge. "The team has needed a defensive midfielder for three years. If you analyse the midfield, they are all naturally attacking players."

At Liverpool, the focus in the remaining days of the transfer window is clear. Their stance is unchanged in that the priority remains wide attacking players rather than midfield, even after the exit of Curtis Jones.

As always, if an opportunity presents itself in the market then Liverpool will consider it but Iraola is understood to be satisfied with his depth in midfield - with Wataru Endo, Trey Nyoni and James McConnell as the back-up options.

Liverpool have previously enquired about Adam Wharton but Crystal Palace's stance is that the 22-year-old is not for sale.

Under Jurgen Klopp, Liverpool tried to get Moises Caicedo in 2023 and when Arne Slot arrived in 2024, Liverpool were keen on signing Martin Zubimendi from Real Sociedad.

But that fell through when the now-Arsenal midfielder turned the move down.

Gravenberch had a brilliant season under Slot as Liverpool cruised their way to the Premier League title, perhaps masking the issues temporarily by covering over emerging cracks.

Liverpool's summer window 12 months ago then became about super-charging their attack with Alexander Isak, Florian Wirtz and Hugo Ekitike, rather than reinforcing the middle of the pitch.

Those fault lines are much clearer now and Iraola will know that his midfield must become harder to break down or else his side will keep on conceding.

title: How to follow Thursday's Champions League draw - and who is in each pot?
description: BBC Sport's Ask Me Anything team explains when the league phase draw for the 2026-27 Champions League is, as well as looking at who is in each pot
fullText:
The league phase draw for the 2026-27 Champions League campaign takes place on Thursday, 27 August at 17:00 BST in Monaco.

A total of 36 teams will enter that stage of the competition and while 29 teams qualified at the end of last season, the remaining seven places were decided by play-offs.

In the league phase, each team will face eight different teams once, with four home matches and four away matches.

For the draw, the 36 teams will be placed into four pots with one being the highest-ranked and four being the lowest. The pot placements are based on the club's Uefa club coefficient ranking from the five-season period ending at the conclusion of 2025-26.

Each team will face two teams from each of the four pots and cannot face a team from the same country as themselves.

Uefa announced a new rule on Wednesday that sides cannot host the same team in three successive league phases - so Liverpool will not draw Real Madrid at home and Arsenal will not travel to Inter Milan. Those fixtures could be drawn in reverse though.

The teams who finish in the top eight will qualify for the Champions League's round of 16. Those between ninth and 24th will enter the play-off knockout round. The 12 teams ranked between 25th and 36th will exit the competition when the league phase is concluded.

Premier League clubs Liverpool, Manchester City and Arsenal all feature in pot one alongside back-to-back Champions League winners Paris St-Germain, Bayern Munich, Real Madrid, Inter Milan, Barcelona and Atletico Madrid.

Aston Villa and Manchester United both return to the Champions League this season after not featuring last term. They are in pot two with Borussia Dortmund, Roma, Sporting, Porto, Club Brugge, Real Betis and PSV Eindhoven.

Pot three consists of Feyenoord, Lille, Bodo/Glimt, Napoli, RB Leipzig, Villarreal, Shakhtar Donetsk, Galatasaray and Fenerbahce.

Slavia Prague, VfB Stuttgart, Lask, Como, Lens, Sabah, AEK Athens, Slovan Bratislava and Viking make up pot four.

title: Federal judge lifts all blocks on Trump mail-in ballots executive order
description: The decision removes legal holds on implementing the president's order.
fullText:
A federal judge who blocked the most controversial aspect of President Donald Trump's executive order aimed at restricting mail-in ballots -- namely, employing the Postal Service as the primary enforcer of mail-voter eligibility -- has now lifted that decision following the Supreme Court's ruling Monday that legal challenges are premature.

The move means there are no longer legal holds on any aspect of Trump's March 2026 mail-in ballot executive order and that the administration is free to move forward, for now, with its implementation without caveats.

Trump's executive order directs the Department of Homeland Security to build a federal citizenship list and give it to the states; the Department of Justice to target state officials who give ballots to noncitizens; and the USPS to direct states to abide by certain mail-ballot design and tracking requirements.

Most critically, the order would require states to provide a list of registered eligible voters to USPS for verification and mandate that postal workers only deliver ballots to persons on the list.

Dozens of Democratic state attorneys general sued the Trump administration over the USPS directive in April, arguing it is unconstitutional since states — not the federal government -- have primary authority for administering elections.

A separate lawsuit by voting rights advocates challenged the proposed USPS ballot verification scheme.

The Supreme Court ruled Monday that the states lacked standing to challenge Trump's order at this stage since nothing had formally impacted how they will administer elections.

The conservative majority made clear, however, that the decision "does not mean that any measure taken by the government to implement the order will necessarily be lawful. On that score, time will tell."

Trump casts mail ballot again in Florida despite efforts to restrict mail voting

The Postal Service this week published its finalized plan with respect to the November election, focusing largely on state ballot design and barcode tracking requirements. Notably, it leaves out or waters down the most controversial aspects envisioned by Trump's order.

At this time, states are not being asked to provide detailed voter eligibility lists to USPS that include personal identifiable information, including citizenship. The USPS also says outright it "will not play any role in determining voter eligibility, maintaining voter rolls, or counting ballots."

The Postal Service, however, will soon proceed with directing states to ensure their mail ballots comport with certain design standards -- including a barcode -- and to provide voter address information to verify delivery.

Twenty-five states filed a new legal challenge against the Postal Service on Wednesday, alleging it is illegal.

"It displaces state laws adopted pursuant to each State's constitutional authority to administer elections, erects new USPS functions and ballot mail constraints that are inconsistent with USPS's governing statutes, flouts USPS's procedural requirements, violates the Privacy Act, and cannot be reconciled with federal voting rights law," they wrote in a lawsuit filed in a Massachusetts District Court.

title: Mini doughnuts sold nationwide recalled. See affected product
description: Packages of mini doughnuts sold nationwide are being recalled after a consumer reported an allergic reaction. Here's what to know.
fullText:
Packages of mini doughnuts sold nationwide are being recalled after a consumer reported an allergic reaction in connection with the treats.

According to U.S. Food and Drug Administration, the Better Bakehouse Snack Company is recalling certain lots of Donutful Chocolate Dipped Vanilla Cake Donuts because the product may contain "undeclared milk." People who have an allergy or severe sensitivity to milk run the risk of serious or life-threatening allergic reaction if they consume this product, the agency said.

The recalled doughnuts are limited to a specific lot of product manufactured and distributed in March 2026, according to the FDA, and the product was shipped to retailers nationwide and through Amazon.

The individual who suffered the allergic reaction has fully recovered, and the manufacturer has identified the cause of the mislabeling issue and has taken corrective measures, the FDA said in its recall report.

According to the FDA, here's what consumers should check for to see if their doughnuts are affected by the recall:

Description: Donutful Chocolate Dipped Vanilla Cake Donuts, 10 Mini Donuts, packaged in a 7.05 oz Carton Containing 5, 1.41 oz (40g) Pouches

Best If Used By Date: 9/15/2026

The FDA says consumers should dispose of the affected product and obtain a refund from their point of purchase with a receipt or return the product for a refund.

Consumers with questions may contact the Better Bakehouse Snack Company at 800-243-0335, Monday through Friday, 9 a.m. ET through 4 p.m. ET.

title: Villa close to £65m move for Chelsea's Jackson
description: The striker is nearing a move to Villa Park after three years at Chelsea.
fullText:
Aston Villa are close to an agreement to sign striker Nicolas Jackson from Chelsea in a deal worth up to £65m.

There is a broad agreement between the clubs over the terms of a move for the 25-year-old, with Chelsea set to achieve their asking price with an initial sum of £47.5m with £17.5m in add-ons.

And if the Senegal international agrees personal terms and completes the switch to Villa his arrival is likely to trigger England international Ollie Watkins' move to Saudi Pro League side Al-Hilal.

The deal remains subject to personal terms being agreed, but negotiations are at an advanced stage, with Jackson expected to reunite with Unai Emery having played under the Villa boss at Spanish club Villarreal.

Jackson would become the latest player in Villa's summer rebuild following the arrivals of record buy Johan Manzambi, midfielder Joao Gomes, goalkeeper Zion Suzuki and defender Matteo Ruggeri.

However, there has also been significant movement out of the club and Watkins leaving would mean they had sold five of the starting XI who won the Europa League in May.

Morgan Rogers, Youri Tielemans, Lucas Digne and Ezri Konsa have already left with goalkeeper Emiliano Martinez expected to depart too.

Chelsea are weighing up a move for the Argentine, who is now deemed surplus to requirements after Suzuki joined from Parma.

In signing Jackson, Villa would be getting a forward who joined Chelsea from Villarreal for £35m in 2023 and scored 30 goals in 81 appearances.

His most recent appearance for the Blues came against Fluminense in the Club World Cup in 2025, while he also won the Europa Conference League with the club.

He spent last season on loan to Bayern Munich, scoring 11 times in 34 games and helping Bayern win the Bundesliga.

Chelsea banked a £14.3m loan fee from the move, though an obligation to buy for £56.2m was not triggered after Jackson failed to make 40 appearances of 45 minutes or more.

Fellow forward Liam Delap is also likely to leave the Blues, with a £50m fee agreed with Nottingham Forest for the striker.

Meanwhile, the club have also been holding talks with Atalanta's Honest Ahanor, 18, over a potential move to Stamford Bridge. The defender is valued at £34.3m by the Italian club.

title: Itauma 'million times better' than Fury and Joshua - Hamed
description: British boxing legend Prince Naseem Hamed has described Moses Itauma as "a million times better" than Anthony Joshua and Tyson Fury.
fullText:
Boxing legend Prince Naseem Hamed has described Moses Itauma as "a million times better" than Anthony Joshua and Tyson Fury and expects the young British heavyweight to surpass both former world champions.

Itauma, 21, is unbeaten in 14 professional fights and faces Croatia's Filip Hrgovic for the vacant IBF heavyweight title at London's O2 Arena on Saturday.

The Chatham fighter has been touted as the heir to the heavyweight throne, while Joshua and Fury have agreed to meet later this year in their long-awaited all-British showdown.

"Moses is on another level to the likes of Tyson Fury and Tyson would say that himself. Tyson would not want to fight Moses and neither would Joshua," Hamed told BBC Sport.

"If they did I would say they are very brave."

Hrgovic taunts starting to wind me up - Itauma

Itauma v Hrgovic & Mayer v Cameron - all you need to know

Victory would make Itauma the second-youngest heavyweight world champion in history, behind only Mike Tyson.

He will also do it one fight sooner than Joshua did when he won his maiden world title in his 16th pro bout.

Fury has lost twice - both to Oleksandr Usyk - while Joshua has lost four times in 34 pro fights.

"I think Tyson Fury was amazing for British boxing and what he achieved, what he did and brought to the game and how colourful he was as a personality," Hamed, 52, added.

"I think Joshua did an amazing job early in his career to win a world title and be an ambassador for British boxing.

"[But] I can't compare Moses. He is a million times better than them."

Hamed was one of British boxing's biggest stars during the 1990s, combining an entertaining fighting style with elaborate ring entrances and a larger-than-life character.

The Sheffield-born fighter became Britain's youngest world champion when he beat Steve Robinson for the WBO featherweight title in Cardiff in 1995, aged 21 and 230 days.

Itauma will miss out on that record by 14 days if he beats Hrgovic.

Hamed, though, says he is not concerned about records and simply wants to see "special fighter" Itauma fulfil his potential.

"Winning a national title as an amateur aged 11 and then having in your head all the way through your amateur career that you'll be world champion at 21 - I visualised that. I think it's very much the same for Moses," he said.

"I'm so confident that Moses is going to be the heavyweight champion of the world. I'm so confident that he'll defend that belt for as long as he wants.

Hrgovic is an underdog despite his superior record against better opposition. The 34-year-old is an Olympic bronze medalist and has only lost once - to current WBO world champion Daniel Dubois in 2024 - in 21 fights.

But Hamed does not expect the fight to prove particularly difficult for Itauma.

"On paper it's a test but I don't think the night that we watch it it will be a test," he said.

"I think it's going to be one of Moses' easiest nights of his career and he'll win a world title."

title: Super Bowl champions Seahawks to be sold in record $9.6bn deal
description: NFL owners approve the $9.612bn record sale of the reigning Super Bowl champions Seattle Seahawks to a group led by billionaire Vinod Khosla.
fullText:
NFL owners have approved the $9.612bn record sale of the reigning Super Bowl champions Seattle Seahawks to a group led by billionaire Vinod Khosla.

The deal, which required the support of at least 24 of 32 owners, is currently the second highest amount paid for a franchise in North American sports history.

The estate of Paul G. Allen, which inherited the NFL team after the death of the Microsoft co-founder in 2018, agreed to terms with the Khosla family on 11 July after a search for a new owner.

And now approved, the sale surpasses the $6.05bn the Washington Commanders fetched when they were sold in 2023, although the NBA's Los Angeles Lakers were subsequently sold for $10bn in 2025 and are currently in the process of changing ownership again for a reported $12.5bn.

"We are honoured to be entrusted as the next stewards of the Seattle Seahawks. How often do you get to buy a franchise that just won the Super Bowl?" said Khosla.

"We are incredibly lucky and humbled by this gift, I would say, from the Allen trust."

"We look forward to building on the winning legacy Paul Allen created and to earning the trust of the Seahawks organisation and fans everywhere."

Speaking at a press conference on Wednesday, Khosla, who will have to relinquish a minority stake in the San Francisco 49ers as part of his agreement to buy the Seahawks, added: "The task ahead is actually pretty simple - keep the winning streak alive, get another Super Bowl.

"Our approach is generally going to be long-term focused, that's our inclination always. So, keep winning, take a long-term approach, and learn a lot. We don't know enough, and the other owners have been incredibly welcoming and willing to teach us, so we'll learn a lot.

"We'll learn from management and see what they are recommending."

title: Uefa to push to remove Infantino after dropping boycott
description: Uefa dropped their plans to boycott Fifa tournaments on Wednesday, but will still move forward with efforts to remove Gianni Infantino.
fullText:
Uefa will press on with its attempt to remove Gianni Infantino as Fifa president despite withdrawing the threat to boycott competitions.

The 55 member associations, plus Europe's members on the Fifa Council, will on Thursday be presented with a letter which guarantees the Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) plan will not be revived.

The official removal of the boycott will be confirmed at Uefa's executive committee meeting in Monaco.

That will satisfy Uefa's demands and mean the Fifa Under-20 Women's World Cup can go ahead next week in Poland with six European teams.

But BBC Sport understands Uefa is confident that a unity candidate can be found to stand against Infantino when he is up for re-election in March.

The vote is likely to be close, with the backing of 106 of the 211 member associations needed to be elected.

However, Uefa has abandoned the idea of trying to force a vote of no confidence.

It would require three quarters of the member associations, 159 votes, to pass the motion, which is considered unrealistic.

No candidate has been identified, though Concacaf president Victor Montagliani is considered a serious option.

Nominations must be submitted by 18 November.

BBC Sport understands that any vote is expected to be close, and for that reason even if Infantino was to win it could cause terminal damage to his presidency, with his legitimacy compromised.

Last month, European football's 55 member associations voted to boycott all Fifa competitions until the FFE proposal was dropped "in its entirety and binding assurances have been given that Fifa will never again open its governance or competitions to private ownership".

After the boycott was dropped, Fifa welcomed the development, saying it is "pleased that all qualified teams will be participating in the upcoming Under-20 Women's World Cup".

Six European teams - England, France, Italy, Portugal, Spain and hosts Poland - are scheduled to play in the tournament.

A Fifa spokesperson said it "strongly believes that football has the power to unite, even in challenging circumstances" and Fifa "remains committed" to developing the game in "full dialogue with the confederations and stakeholders".

'Change is necessary' - players unite against Fifa

Uefa chief Ceferin rules out Fifa presidency bid

On Tuesday, a group of former players published a statement saying "change is necessary" at the head of Fifa.

Former Manchester United and France defender Mikael Silvestre, who sits on Fifa's Players' Voice Panel, issued a statement on X on Monday in a post he titled "Enough is Enough!".

The statement has been shared on social media by the likes of England defender Lucy Bronze, France's 1998 World Cup winner Emmanuel Petit and former England goalkeeper David James.

However on Wednesday, a different group of former players including World Cup-winning Brazil captain Cafu, former Italy striker Christian Vieri, former Portugal captain Pepe and ex-Argentina international Esteban Cambiasso all posted supportive messages for Infantino on social media.

All of the players are so-called Fifa Legends, officially recognised by the governing body.

Vieri's statement said: "Over the past 10 years, we have seen the work Fifa and President Infantino have done to create representativity for players in football, which did not exist.

"We will remain available to support the great evolution our game has seen this past decade, so that it keeps reaching and benefiting people of every country that plays football all around the world."

title: Watson to face fellow Briton Dart for US Open spot
description: Heather Watson will face compatriot Harriet Dart for a place in the US Open main draw as six British players reach the final qualifying round.
fullText:

title: Bill Gates diagnoses problems with AI, but an expert questions his prescription
description: "There is no plan to ease the entry into the AI era," Gates writes in an essay.
fullText:
He helped pioneer the personal computer revolution, but Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates is hitting the panic button on artificial intelligence, writing in an essay that AI is forging the "most turbulent time in human history."

The 70-year-old Gates issued an urgent warning in the nearly 6,000-word essay published Wednesday on his personal website.

He predicts massive unemployment and economic turmoil, and spells out the consequences of AI falling into the hands of criminals if U.S. and global leaders do not immediately work together to address the dark side of the technology.

"In terms of equity, AI will either be the greatest equalizer ever invented, or the worst source of injustice. The challenge is monumental," Gates wrote in his essay. "Even under the best circumstances, the transition to this new AI era will be one of the most turbulent times in human history."

Gates is the latest tech titan to sound the alarm on the rapid development of AI, and he echoed many concerns others have raised.

In an interview with ABC News in June, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei warned that AI needs to be developed with the proper guardrails to ensure it has a positive impact on the world.

"We're proposing stronger regulation of the technology, proposing giving the government the ability to, again, in a narrow way, block deployment of unsafe technology," Amodei told ABC News.

In June, President Donald Trump signed an executive order that requests AI companies share products with the federal government for evaluation before a wider release.

In an interview with The New York Times published Wednesday, Gates alleged that tech industry executives are knowingly downplaying the threats of AI, suggesting they are putting profits over precautions.

OpenAI pauses some AI training after autonomous cyberattack

"In private, people who understand how good this stuff is, and how much better it's getting, they're very worried," said Gates, adding that few tech executives would publicly admit that. "They're now saying to each other: 'Hey, man, don't say that. It's bad for us -- the next trillion dollars we're trying to raise."

In his essay, Gates said that advances in AI are moving at a "mind-blowing rate."

"AI for the first time can replace and exceed human cognition," Gates wrote, adding that soon "it will be substantially better than humans at many tasks."

He said that the rapid improvements in the technology raise questions such as how to keep it "from widening the divide between rich and poor?" and how to "protect the people who are most vulnerable to the harms of artificial intelligence, including those who lose their livelihoods and the sense that they are in control of their future?"

Gates said that answering these questions "should be the world's top priority."

"Unfortunately, right now we are not preparing for it," Gates wrote. "I don't see evidence that leaders, experts, and communities are confronting the challenges adequately. There is no plan to ease the entry into the AI era."

He said the AI era is far different than the personal computer revolution, which took 20 years to significantly change how people adapted to working with PCs.

'I was foolish': Bill Gates denies wrongdoing after latest release of Epstein files

"If someone had a credible plan for slowing down AI advances globally, I would likely support it," Gates wrote. "However, I don't think that's going to happen. The geopolitical and economic incentives are pushing too hard to go full speed ahead."

His essay Wednesday comes years after an interview with ABC News, where Gates seemed to reject pausing AI technology until some guardrails are established.

"If you just pause the good guys and you don't pause everyone else, you're probably hurting yourself. You definitely want the good guys to have strong AI," Gates said in the 2023 interview.

Now, Gates is saying it is imperative to think of how to reduce job losses. He suggested several ways of slowing the advances of the technology, including imposing a tax on AI tokens, which are used by AI companies to track usage and bill customers. He also said there should be a tax on robots that are used to replace human workers.

"Right now, if you're an employer and you hire someone, you have to pay taxes on their earnings, but if you buy a robot, you can usually write it off right away as a business expense," Gates wrote.

He suggested that such taxes would "slow the rush away from human labor," while raising money for retraining displaced human workers and providing them with stronger safety nets.

Gates also suggested preserving some jobs for what he called a "human reserved domain," such as caregivers, mental health workers and some medical professionals.

"Imagine a robot giving you the awful news that you have an incurable disease. There's no technical reason why it couldn't. Yet it shouldn't," Gates wrote.

Oren Etzioni, a computer science professor at the University of Washington, said he agreed with much of what Gates wrote in his essay.

"I think he has the diagnosis right, but the prescription wrong, at least in some places," Etzioni said in a phone interview with ABC News on Wednesday.

Etzioni is also the founding CEO of the Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence, which was funded by the late Paul Allen, Gates' Microsoft co-founder.

He said that while it makes sense for Congress to impose a tax on robots that replace workers, he is less supportive of taxes on AI tokens.

"I think that taxing tokens is like taxing keystrokes on a typewriter. It doesn't make sense. It measures effort, not displacement of workers," Etzioni said. "I think that's an example where we need much better ideas."

Etzioni said taxing to slow the advances of AI is also tricky.

"We have to keep an eye on our adversaries. You tax what you want less of. You tax what you want to happen more slowly," Etzioni said. "This is a tax in a highly competitive environment. So if we slow down, do we get overtaken? And, in fact, if we tax American tokens, then what happens when people use Chinese models? Are we shipping AI use offshore with these taxes?"

He also said that pumping the brakes on AI technology until policies and global agencies are created to control it flies in the face of another statement Gates made in his essay, when he wrote, "We do not have the luxury of moving slowly."

"My suggestion would be, to the extent possible, certainly in the U.S., we don't need new government agencies. What we need is for existing agencies to enact the right policies," Etzioni said.

Etzioni said an important thing to keep in mind is that it's not too late to address the problems AI is creating.

"Even three years ago, we didn't know what was happening and how fast it was happening. So it's not too late now," Etizoni said. "Let's make sure that we act with urgency and pragmatism because it may well be too late three years from now."

title: Testimony concludes in Lindsay Clancy’s murder trial. Jury to hear closing arguments Thursday
description: Testimony concluded Wednesday in the murder trial of Lindsay Clancy, a mother accused of strangling her three young children in a case that has drawn attention to postpartum mental health.  Closing ar...
fullText:
Testimony concluded Wednesday in the murder trial of Lindsay Clancy, a mother accused of strangling her three young children in a case that has drawn attention to postpartum mental health.

Closing arguments are expected to begin Thursday, before the jury begins deliberating.

Clancy, 36, has pleaded not guilty by reason of lack of criminal responsibility, with her lawyers arguing she was experiencing postpartum psychosis when she killed 5-year-old Cora, 3-year-old Dawson and 8-month-old Callan Clancy at the family's home in coastal Duxbury, Massachusetts, in January 2023. The rare mental illness is linked to the stress, sleep deprivation and hormonal changes that follow childbirth.

EDITOR'S NOTE: This story includes discussion of suicide. If you or someone you know needs help, the national suicide and crisis lifeline in the U.S. is available by calling or texting 988.

Prosecutors say Clancy planned the killings and understood her actions were wrong.

Clancy did not testify during the trial, which is in its fifth week. The defense called 10 witnesses, including some of Clancy's friends and relatives, while prosecutors called more than 70 witnesses, including her then-husband.

Testifying as the final rebuttal witness for the prosecution, a forensic psychiatrist at the University of Virginia and a senior psychiatrist for the FBI's Behavioral Analysis Unit said Wednesday that he did not believe Clancy's account that a voice ordered her to kill the children.

Prosecutor Jennifer Sprague asked Dr. Gregory Saathoff a series of questions about Clancy's account: Did the voice tell her where to kill the children? How to kill them? What to use? In what order? Saathoff answered no each time.

"Having no instructions as to how to do it, but being able to execute those decisions … that is surprising that she's able to accomplish all of this without any other kind of direction or plan," he said.

All three children were strangled with exercise bands in the family's basement before Clancy tried to kill herself while her husband was getting takeout and at a pharmacy on Jan. 24, 2023. Saathoff said her ability to accomplish everything she did without direction indicated Clancy "had control, control of the sequence of what she was doing throughout."

"In the small amount of time that Miss Clancy had in the home without her husband, it was important, in order to carry this out, as well as her suicide, to do this quickly, methodically, and alike," he said.

On Tuesday, Saathoff said he found it unusual that Clancy said the voice stopped once she was done strangling the children, that the voice was constant rather than intermittent and that she never previously reported hearing a voice to her medical providers. She also gave a different timeline to other evaluators about when she first heard the voice that day, he said.

"Committing the act is not curative of the voice," Saathoff said of the voice stopping abruptly. "I've not ever seen that."

Defense attorney Kevin Reddington began his cross-examination of Saathoff on Wednesday by trying to cast doubt on Saathoff's expertise in postpartum psychosis and portray him as someone closely aligned with law enforcement, questioning him about his work with prisons, the Justice Department and the Virginia attorney general's office.

Saathoff testified that he treated women with postpartum psychosis while working at a state hospital in the 1980s and 1990s, while much of his more recent research has focused on such subjects as extremist violence, national security and political radicalization.

Reddington also asked Saathoff about Clancy's attempts to search online for information about postpartum depression, her visits to multiple maternal and mental health providers, disclosures to her mother and then-husband that she was suicidal and feared that she would harm her children, and calls to a suicide hotline — all attempts that Reddington contended establish Clancy realized something was seriously wrong and made a sincere effort over time to get help.

Reddington asked whether Saathoff believes that Clancy decided to kill her children because she "no longer liked the life she thought she wanted" and was making "a selfish choice" to "manipulate her providers, seek out a quick and easy fix when she was feeling depressed and anxious."

"I think that statement that you read really minimizes what she was going through," Saathoff responded.

title: Vrancken's side come of age as Hearts bid goodnight Vienna
description: After some early season setbacks, "proud" Wouter Vrancken believes Hearts are getting their rewards by securing Conference League progress.
fullText:
If 16 May was the day the dream ended, 26 August may well turn out to be when the next one started for Hearts.

A mere three months on from a final-day defeat that denied Hearts a first Scottish top-flight title in 66 years, they have not only secured a tangible reward for finishing as runners-up, they did so with immense courage and togetherness.

Thursday's victory over Rapid Vienna on penalties secured a place in Friday's league phase draw for the Conference League and two games each in October, November and December.

A lot has changed in that three months - a new head coach in Belgian Wouter Vrancken, player departures and plenty arrivals - and a sticky start to the season threatened to prolong a sense of malaise after that 3-1 defeat by champions Celtic.

European and domestic losses got the 2026-27 campaign off to a whimper but Vrancken stayed calm and believes his team are now reaping deserved benefits.

"They have to learn that they're a good team, that they're good players, that they can show it," he told BBC Scotland.

"In the last away games in Europe, you see that they're a little bit scared to do things, to take risks or to give spaces away. Then we don't play our game.

"The development of the team, the progress of the team is amazing. The team spirit, I saw it from the first session already.

"They want to learn it. They wanted to have feedback. They want to go into it and the kind of football we played. This is the result. They get rewarded and I'm so happy for them."

Heroic Hearts beat Rapid Vienna on penalties to secure Conference League progress

Visit our Hearts page for all the latest news, analysis and fan views

While the margin of Hearts' 6-0 aggregate loss to Sturm Graz in the Champions League second qualifying round may have been unexpected, the result was not much of a surprise.

Even less surprising was losing to Benfica, typically a Champions League team, in the Europa League qualifiers, though again the margin was heavy at 7-1 on aggregate.

Facing Rapid Vienna in the Conference League play-off represented another tough tie, though not considered as tough as either Sturm Graz or Benfica.

Roughly this time last year, Dundee United took Rapid to penalties in their Conference League qualifying tie but lost in the shootout and the improvement in Hearts' domestic form after a losing start at Aberdeen raised hopes that European league phase football was achievable.

Hearts more than gave as good as they got in the first leg, but the absence of a lead to take over to Austria made Rapid slight favourites at 2-2, more so after Ercan Kara gave them a 1-0 lead on the night at the Allianz Stadion.

A Tomas Magnusson red card for Hearts preceded the Pierre Landry Kabore equaliser that forced extra time. Calvin Miller's volley very nearly secured them the win only for Nenad Cvetkovic to level for Rapid on 119 minutes.

A first save in the shootout from Beau Reus to deny Moulaye Haidara put Hearts within touching distance again but Oisin McEntee's spot-kick getting blocked prolonged the tension.

Up stepped Marco Tilio, a former Celtic winger perhaps with a point to prove after a frustrating spell in Glasgow. But it was Reus who had the last word with another terrific stop to secure a 4-3 win on penalties.

Vrancken's post-match comments revealed how much he believes his side have come in a short space of time.

"When you see the game, we played a really bad first half, a little bit similar as we did in Benfica," he explained.

"We made agreements, we had a game plan and we didn't follow up, we didn't show the guts to follow up.

"When you play against a side like Rapid Vienna, when you don't show it, they can play through you. We were already pretty angry at half-time and we came out, we did much better.

"We took the game in our hands, we were dominant at that moment. This is already a mental strength, coming back on 1-0 down and coming back like this.

"Again, in the extra time, you try to take the game with you to Hearts and to Edinburgh, then you get a mental kick again in the last minute of the extra time.

"Again, I'm so proud of these guys that they stay in the game, focused and concentrated to win the penalties.

"We can make more steps in the coming weeks and hope that we can take the steps as soon as possible."

Progress in Europe brings obvious financial rewards and there may be sales as well as purchases at Hearts in the closing days of the transfer window.

Hearts have already brought in 12 new players this summer while even more than that have moved on.

Now with at least six more European fixtures to play this season, former Hearts player Ryan Stevenson believes the club will have to recruit.

"I think they'll definitely need to bring in another two or three anyway when you look at the League Cup, the six games in Europe, the league, which is so important," he told BBC Radio Scotland's Sportsound.

Another former Tynecastle favourite, Allan Preston, believes Hearts will be prepared for such a task.

"They've got people ready to come if they're needed," he said. "They are ready. They don't wait until things happen. They already do things.

"If they need to, they'll be pushing the button before the transfer window closes. They will get better, they'll produce better."

One position Hearts may have to look at as a priority is midfield after Tom Renaud's first-half injury.

"That's the biggest disappointment of the evening," lamented Vrancken.

"It's not looking good but I hope for him that it's OK. We have to look there because he was also really good in the last game.

"We're talking every day about those things and we'll see in the next weeks."

title: 'Mini-Rodri' Gonzalez shown he will be loved at Newcastle
description: Nico Gonzalez is given a rapturous welcome before Newcastle's Carabao Cup win against West Brom following the £52m midfielder's arrival from Manchester City.
fullText:
Nico Gonzalez wanted to feel loved. He quickly got his wish at St James' Park on Wednesday night after completing his £52m move from Manchester City.

Newcastle United's new signing was handed a rapturous welcome before he even kicked a ball for the club as supporters repeatedly chanted his name.

The sight of Gonzalez walking out at the sold-out stadium before the 3-2 win against West Bromwich Albion in the Carabao Cup second round was a welcome one for head coach Matthias Jaissle, who desperately wanted him.

The German stressed he was "always a believer in the positive things", but tellingly also referred to the pursuit as a "long fight".

Having spoken personally to Gonzalez on a number of occasions, Jaissle made it clear how much he wanted the 24-year-old and how pivotal he would be in his side.

"It's always important if you're making signings like Nico that there is a commitment there," Jaissle said.

"But he showed that from the beginning, from our first conversations."

Newcastle face Millwall in third round - full draw

A lot has clearly changed since Gonzalez first set foot in the Premier League a year and a half ago and made his Manchester City debut against Newcastle. Of all teams.

Before City's 4-0 win, the new arrival had been warned about the intensity Newcastle's midfielders played and pressed with at their snarling best.

But the unfazed Spaniard ended up completing a staggering 100 passes, and helped snuff out any potential breakaways from the visitors at Etihad Stadium.

It was a glimpse of the skillset - in and out of possession - which convinced Manchester City to sign defensive midfielder Gonzalez from Porto for £50m.

City's then manager, Pep Guardiola, even labelled him "our mini-Rodri" in the absence of his influential, injured team-mate.

Gonzalez ultimately found an extended run of starts hard to come by once his compatriot returned to full fitness, though.

But former Manchester City assistant manager Kolo Toure believes he will have benefited from his experience at the Etihad.

"When you are in competition against players like Rodri, you learn a lot because you come up against them in training and you have to show the manager you are better than them," he said.

"You learn from things they do as well and, on the ball, he learned a lot from Rodri. Without the ball he's really good because he can press, get it back and read the game really well.

"He has this capacity to steal the ball from opponents, which is top. He's better than Rodri at this in my opinion, but Rodri on the ball is the best in the world.

"Both of them have different qualities and different strengths."

Gonzalez had a close relationship with Rodri and long humbly recognised that only a select number of players can start in his position at clubs bidding to challenge for the biggest honours.

Rodri was that man at Manchester City under Guardiola and, following the midfielder's move to Barcelona, new manager Enzo Maresca has signed Ayyoub Bouaddi from Lille, having already brought in Elliot Anderson from Nottingham Forest.

The club also look set to make a bid for Chelsea's Enzo Fernandez.

It was still not easy for Gonzalez to leave Manchester City, where he felt settled, but Newcastle will give him the platform he has been longing for as a key player.

The enthusiastic Spaniard sees this as an opportunity to develop further, which has always been a driver.

"His mentality is top," Toure said. "I would review games individually with the players and every time I had my laptop and sat next to him, he was so open to learning.

"He wanted me to show him and I wanted to help him because he was demanding in that way.

"You want to have players like this because they want to see what they do well and not well, and are open to criticism.

"He's going to keep on improving because of his mentality."

Gonzalez certainly did so when he left Barcelona, where his professional career started, and has such experience to fall back on.

Having spent a decade at Barca, and risen through the ranks, Gonzalez ultimately had to depart to truly flourish elsewhere.

Following a successful loan spell at Valencia, he joined Porto on a permanent basis at the age of 21 before earning a move to Manchester City.

Former Barcelona B team-mate Roger Riera feels he has developed "another vision" as a result.

"Nico has seen different countries and different styles of football," he said. "He's added a lot of things to his game, which have made him a more complete player.

Barnes scores twice as Newcastle survive West Brom scare

Signs that Jaissle's Newcastle are not to be written off

title: Is Saka getting back to his best at Arsenal?
description: Bukayo Saka has struggled to produce his best on a consistent basis in recent months, but could be getting back to top form this season.
fullText:
Bukayo Saka's performance in Arsenal's impressive opening-day win has already convinced some fans the Gunners are going to defend their Premier League crown.

The 24-year-old's game-time for the north London outfit was managed at the end of last season, as well as with England at the World Cup, because of an Achilles injury he picked up in March.

Saka missed the March international break and seven games for the Gunners, but returned to help them lift the Premier League title for the first time in 22 years.

The winger was then taken off during the Champions League final as Arsenal lost to Paris-St Germain in Budapest and his performance was criticised.

England boss Thomas Tuchel also limited his minutes during the World Cup, but asked if he found it frustrating being judged while not 100% fit, Saka said it was a "gamble" he was willing to take.

A rest after the tournament seems to have allowed Saka to start this campaign at his best. He looked sharp against newly promoted Coventry on Friday, giving full-back Jay Dasilva a torrid time while scoring the second goal in the 3-0 win.

The sight of Saka flying down the right wing and involved in a lot of Arsenal's attacks will be welcomed by supporters.

Because, despite a stop-start season last year, Saka still clocked up 49 appearances for the Gunners and their win percentage was notably more impressive with him in the team.

Saka only started three of England's eight games at the World Cup, including scoring a hat-trick in the 6-4 third-place final win over France.

That result secured England's best finish in a World Cup on foreign soil.

Saka, though, had been left out of the semi-final defeat by Argentina, despite starting the last-16 win over Mexico and the quarter-final win over Norway.

The winger said after the victory against Mexico he wished he had been at 100% fitness going into the tournament but accepted "that hasn't been the case".

Saka played just 357 minutes at the World Cup, just 48% of England's total minutes across eight matches at the tournament.

He showed flashes of his quality, providing three assists, which alongside Anthony Gordon was the most of any England player, as well as three goals.

In fact, he registered a goal involvement on average every 60 minutes for the Three Lions during the tournament.

Alvarez's Arsenal dilemma amid summer's most bitter transfer tussle

Al-Hilal in advanced talks to sign Arsenal's Martinelli

Saka returned from the World Cup and after a break rejoined the Arsenal squad, playing his first minutes of this season in the Community Shield, coming on when the Gunners were already leading Manchester City 3-0.

His acceleration and sharpness during that cameo was something that was lacking towards the end of last season as the winger looked to help his team get over the line.

And after his starring performance against Coventry in the first Premier League game of the season, he hinted that after low minutes at the World Cup and a summer break he felt back to his best.

"I was training a lot so I could be ready for the start of the season and ready to help the team in the way I know I can," Saka said in the mixed zone after the win.

"It was more about balancing my time off and not having too much of a break. I took seven days off and then started to train again.

"I've put in a lot of work since then and I'm feeling good. I just tried to come back in good shape, so I'm on top of my body."

That motivation seems to have come from the frustration of not achieving England's goal at the World Cup, with the winger returning to training a few days early.

"The World Cup didn't necessarily go how I wanted it to, for myself and for the team as well," he said.

"I felt really hungry after the World Cup, after the season ended. I was looking forward to this new season."

Another part of why Saka looks like he is in a flow state so early in the season is the return of Kai Havertz, Martin Odegaard and Ben White to full fitness.

There is no debate that White and Saka's partnership down the right-hand side, with the defender's overlapping runs, unlock the best in Saka.

The partnership he has with Odegaard and Havertz is also crucial to a fluid Arsenal attack and the win over Coventry was just the second time since December 2024 that the trio started a Premier League game together, such have been their injury problems.

There have been questions about whether Arteta is too reliant on Saka, and before the start of this season the winger had played 153 matches, with 61 of them being the full 90 minutes, across the past three seasons.

But with an enforced break through injury and then lower minutes at the World Cup, he could be about to produce the regular scintillating performances we have become used to.
